speaker: wren
lines: You must be Nana's Pip. She said you'd be coming up the valley before the snow.
I'm Wren. I write down what the valley sounds like: the springs, the ice, the pines knocking together.
My book's nearly full now. There's one page left, and I can't think of anything worth putting on it.

speaker: wren
lines: Oh, it's not the page, it's me. Everything I hear sounds like something I've already written down.
The very first page I ever wrote was the mast on Brindle Peak, humming in the cold. I was younger than you are.

speaker: wren
lines: So would you listen for me? You've got fresh ears. Go to the hoarfrost glade and take a photograph there.
Holding still for a picture is about the only time anybody really listens. You'll hear the frost.
Then go down to Kettle Springs and walk in among the hot pools. Nothing else sounds like that water, and you'll hear it as you go.
Then come back and tell me what you heard, and I'll put it on the last page.

speaker: wren
lines: Oh, you're back. Go to the hoarfrost glade first, and hold still for the picture so you can listen.
Then walk in among the hot pools at Kettle Springs and listen there too. Then come and tell me.

speaker: wren
lines: Go to the glade first, for the frost. Then the hot pools at Kettle Springs. And then come back to me.

speaker: wren
lines: You've been to both? Go on, then, tell me. What did you hear?

choices.text: the frost ticked, like a stove cooling down.
the springs sounded like a kettle arguing with itself.

speaker: wren
lines: Like a stove cooling down. Oh, that's exactly it. I'd stopped being able to hear it.
And the springs? No, keep that one to yourself. I'll go down and hear it for myself.

speaker: wren
lines: A kettle arguing with itself. Oh, that's exactly it. I'd stopped being able to hear it.
And the frost? No, keep that one to yourself. I'll go up to the glade and listen for myself.

speaker: wren
lines: There. That's the last page, and the book's full.
You take it. I'll start a new one tomorrow, with my ears washed out.

speaker: tamsin
lines: Oh! Mind the needles, they get everywhere. I'm Tamsin. I knit things.
This is a headband for the hare down by the road head. His ears go flat in the cold, poor thing.
Only I've never measured him. I didn't like to ask. So it might not fit him at all.

choices.text: how will you know if it fits?

speaker: tamsin
lines: Walk up to a hare and ask him to hold still while I measure his ears? I'd rather knit in the dark.
So I guess. I always guess. Would you help me find out whether I guessed right?

speaker: tamsin
lines: He lives down by the road head, in Hearth Hollow. Hollis, he's called.
Would you take it to him and ask him to try it on? I'd only fret if I went myself.
And have a go at the pinecone toss while you're here, if you like. I do enjoy watching someone else be bad at something.
Then come back and tell me if it fits. Honestly, mind. I'd rather know.

speaker: tamsin
lines: Still got it with you? It's for Hollis, the hare by the road head. Ask him to try it on.
And if it's too tight, you tell me. I'd rather know.

speaker: tamsin
lines: It fits? A bit tight on the ears, but it fits? Oh, thank goodness for that.
Then I'll give the next one more room round the ears. You keep this one. It was practice.
And next time, I'll ask him myself. Out loud and everything.

speaker: fen
lines: You're up early. Or late. It's hard to tell from up a pine.
I keep watch over the pines. Everything that moves through here goes down in my tally. Well, nearly everything.

speaker: fen
lines: The wood's full of comings and goings, and somebody ought to keep track of them. It isn't prying if you write it down.
Most folk talk around an owl and hope he'll fill in the rest. I don't, as it happens.

speaker: fen
lines: From this branch I can see the creek. Up the hill there's a deer trail, but the trees hide it from me.
Something comes down that trail every day. I see it go in at the top, but I never see what it is.
If you run the trail, fast, you'll see where it bends, past the glade and the split pine.
Tamsin, the marten who knits by the split pine, sits right at the bend. Ask her what comes past.

speaker: fen
lines: You're back. Run the deer trail for me, fast, and see where it bends.
Then ask Tamsin, by the split pine, what comes down it, and come and tell me.

speaker: fen
lines: Run the deer trail first, fast. Then ask Tamsin, by the split pine. She sees whatever comes past.

speaker: fen
lines: A roe deer? Coming down from the glade to drink at the creek, every morning?
There. That's the last line in my tally.
Twenty winters I've watched this wood, and I could have asked the marten next door any day I liked.

speaker: ilsa
lines: You're Pip, aren't you? Nana's told me all about you. Don't stand still too long, you'll freeze.
I'm Ilsa. I carry things for people. Firewood, parcels, whatever needs carrying.
This one's for my sister. Only we had words, and I'd rather not be the one to take it over.

choices.text: what did you have words about?

speaker: ilsa
lines: She says I carry everybody else's load and then sulk because nobody carries mine.
And I say she sits in her steam and waits for everyone to come to her.
We're both right, which is the worst way to have a row.

speaker: ilsa
lines: My sister Ivy keeps the hot pools at Kettle Springs, down the valley.
Put it in her hands, would you, not on the step. She'll say I should have come myself.
Don't argue with her about it. Just come back and tell me it got there.

speaker: ilsa
lines: Still carrying it? That's all right. Ivy, my sister, is down at the pools, in the steam.
If she starts on about me, don't argue. Just hand it over and tell her it's from me.

speaker: ilsa
lines: It got there? She took it?
And she said I should come down myself. Of course she did.
Well, then. Tomorrow I'll go down there, carrying nothing at all, and let her feed me.
But sit down for a minute first. No, really, sit. I'm practising.

speaker: fen
lines: You asked me straight out. Hardly anybody does that. Most folk drop hints and hope.
I did see it. Hollis, the hare, hung it on a low branch to dry.
The wind took it into the creek pool below the split pine. That's the pine with two tops, standing over the rest, a short walk up the creek from my branch. Fish there and you'll hook it.
I never took it. Tell him that from me. He's been thinking it for two days.

speaker: tamsin
lines: Fen, the owl, wants to know what comes down the deer trail? He could have just asked me.
It's the roe deer from the hoarfrost glade. She comes past my stump every morning on her way down to the creek for a drink.
Tell him that. And tell him he's allowed to come and ask me himself, you know.

speaker: wren
lines: I've started a new book. I write more slowly now, and I listen for longer first.
Listen, can you hear that knocking? That's the pines in the cold. I'd stopped noticing it.
If you hear anything I haven't, come and tell me, and I'll write it down.

speaker: tamsin
lines: I'm knitting him another one. Measured, this time. I asked the hare to hold still, and he did.
It turns out people quite like being asked. Who knew?
Mind the needles on the stump. They're sharper than they look.

speaker: fen
lines: My tally's complete now. A roe deer, every morning, down to the creek.
I asked the marten by the split pine a question yesterday. She talked for an hour. I might do it again.
Ask me something, if you like. I always answer when I'm asked.

speaker: ilsa
lines: I'm going down to see Ivy, my sister, tomorrow. I'm going to let her feed me.
Don't tell her, though. She'll make a big fuss about it, and I'll secretly enjoy every minute.
Sit with me a while. I'm practising sitting still. I'm not very good at it yet.
